[raw_data](raw_data/) contains purchase history up to the end of June 1998 of the cohort of 23,570 individuals who made their first-ever purchase at CDNOW in the first quarter of 1997. See [read_me_CDNOW_master.txt](raw_data/read_me_CDNOW_master.txt) for more context.

Note that the data only gives us customer behaviour for that one cohort and has no information about how much it took to acquire the customers.

Goal is to understand the data an CDnow's revenue, we will go back and forth to form a story using their data. To start, let's plot s chart that shows me for each month, what's the split between initial and repeated purchases.
I’ll check the data notes, then plot monthly revenue split between first and repeat purchases.

The file contains transaction values, so I’ll use dollars for the split. I’ll count each customer’s first transaction as initial revenue and all later transactions as repeat revenue, using file order when dates tie. Initial revenue will stop after March 1997 because this cohort includes only customers acquired in that quarter.

![Monthly revenue split between initial and repeat purchases](../assets/diagrams/cdnow_monthly_initial_repeat_revenue.png)

I’ve interpreted “split” as **revenue in dollars**. Initial means each customer’s first transaction; repeat means every subsequent transaction.

Repeat purchases contributed **12.2%** of January revenue, **26.8%** in February, and **40.4%** in March 1997. From April onward, all revenue is repeat revenue because this cohort stops adding customers after March—this doesn’t describe CDNOW’s company-wide revenue.

[Monthly data](../assets/diagrams/cdnow_monthly_initial_repeat_revenue.csv)

Ok looks like its very dependant on customers coming back. Therefore, we need to know if the returning revenue is just a few high spenders or many returning customers. Plot 2 charts for every month showing how many customers purchased something vs the average cart value per customer.
I’ll plot monthly purchasing customers and average monthly spend per purchasing customer, focusing on repeat purchases to match your question about returning revenue.

![Monthly purchasing customers and average spend per customer](../assets/diagrams/cdnow_monthly_customers_and_spend.png)

The second chart uses **monthly revenue ÷ purchasing customers**, including multiple orders from the same customer.

From April 1997 to June 1998:

- Monthly purchasing customers fell from **2,822 to 1,506**, down **47%**.
- Average monthly spend stayed near **$50 per purchasing customer**.

That suggests the revenue decline mainly reflects fewer customers purchasing each month. These averages don’t establish whether a few high spenders dominate revenue—we’d need to examine spending concentration to answer that.

[Monthly data](../assets/diagrams/cdnow_monthly_customers_and_spend.csv)

ok can't really see much info in this apart from the sharp drop of number of customers at the start. Can we instead combine both of these metrics? I want to take April 1997 as the basline then we calculate every month after that as a percentage up/down from that baseline. This means that April 1997 will be 100% and if May 1997 drops by 50% of April 1997, it will be at 50%. Show me the plot
I’ll put both metrics on one chart, indexed to April 1997 = 100%, and show April 1997 through June 1998.

![Purchasing customers and monthly spend per customer indexed to April 1997](../assets/diagrams/cdnow_monthly_customers_and_spend_indexed.png)

Both metrics start at **100% in April 1997**. By June 1998, purchasing customers were at **53.4%** of the baseline, while monthly spend per purchasing customer remained at **99.9%**.
<external_codex_apps_open_page>{"page_id":null}</external_codex_apps_open_page>
ok if average spent is stable but number of customers go down, this is probably aligned with the monthly revenue. Add that to the plot so that I can just see it in 1 shot
I’ll add monthly revenue to the same chart, also indexed to April 1997 = 100%.

![Monthly revenue, purchasing customers and spend per customer indexed to April 1997 = 100%](../assets/diagrams/cdnow_monthly_customers_and_spend_indexed.png)

Revenue closely follows customer numbers. By June 1998, revenue was **53.3%** of April’s level, purchasing customers were **53.4%**, and spend per customer was **99.9%**.

Ok, that raises 2 questions:
1. Activity over time: if future revenue depends mainly on how many people buy, how does
purchasing activity change as customers get further from their first purchase?
2. Spending concentration: is there a small group contributing much of the revenue?

For point 1, since users start their initial purchase differently, we will need to align users by their 1st purchase then for their repeat purchase, we need to track how many % of customers buy on their subsequent months.

For point 2, just calculate total revenue percentage covered for top  1,5,10,15,20% spending customers.

I’ll align customers by their first-purchase month and plot the percentage who buy in each subsequent month. Month 1 will mean the next calendar month; at longer horizons, I’ll include only customers whose corresponding month is fully observed.

I’ll also rank customers by total revenue across the observed period and calculate the shares contributed by the top 1%, 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20%.

![Purchasing activity since first purchase](../assets/diagrams/cdnow_activity_by_month_since_first_purchase.png)

**Purchasing activity falls quickly, then declines more slowly:** 14.9% buy in the next calendar month, 8.1% in month 6, and 6.3% in month 15.

Each point measures purchasing **during that month**; customers can skip months and return. Months 16–17 include only customers with enough observation time.

![Customer revenue concentration](../assets/diagrams/cdnow_customer_revenue_concentration.png)

| Top spending customers | Share of total revenue |
|---|---:|
| 1% | 15.9% |
| 5% | 36.7% |
| 10% | 50.9% |
| 15% | 60.6% |
| 20% | 67.8% |

**Revenue is concentrated:** the highest-spending 10% contribute just over half. These totals include initial and repeat purchases through June 1998, rather than lifetime spending.

Ok before we continue, I will consolidate conclusions here for fact checking.



Conclusions:

1. Cdnow is very dependent on repeat customers and they do have repeat customers but monthly repeat purchases declines. We see 14.9% of customers repurchase on month 1 but only 6.3% do the same on month 17.
2. Number of customers is not the only metric as we see that the top 10% of customers account for 50.9% of revenue. This means cdnow has to make sure to repeat the ability to attract the same customer profile.

Both are directionally supported, with a few adjustments.

1. **Within this cohort, monthly repeat purchasing activity declines as customers get further from their first purchase.** The percentage buying falls from **14.9% in month 1 to 6.3% in month 15**. Use month 15 because all 23,570 customers are observed through that point; month 17 includes only January entrants. The decline is an overall trend, with some monthly increases. This cohort alone cannot establish how dependent CDNOW’s entire business is on repeat customers.

2. **Customer numbers alone do not capture revenue contribution: the top-spending 10% generated 50.9% of observed revenue.** This supports investigating what distinguishes valuable customers and what drives their repeat spending. However, we haven’t established an identifiable customer profile that CDNOW could repeatedly attract. These customers were ranked using their eventual spending; we would need to test whether information available early predicts that value.

Your proposed acquisition implication is therefore a **hypothesis to investigate**, rather than a conclusion yet. Acquisition costs and margins would also be needed to assess whether attracting those customers is profitable.

Ok now that we understand how CDnow customers work. 



For context, we are evaluating CDnow, an online music retailer where customers can order music CDs to be sent to them. They are seeking cohort based financing for future cohorts, where:

- We would provide them with a fixed amount of capital on a loan basis, fixed to a certain cohort of users (e.g. all users who have purchased their first CD in the 1997Q2). 
- They will use this fixed amount of capital for marketing, advertising, and other distribution related costs. 
- 50% of the revenue from that cohort is then repaid to us, until a cap of 1.2x of the original capital has been returned, after which CDnow has no further obligation.



Let's move on to some basic forecasting. Since only 1 cohort data was given, we can just base off that and do a normal/worse case scenario forecasting. For normal case, we can just replay the the exact same behaviour as the data cohort. For the worse case, let's assume CDnow is unable to capture the same amount and quality of customers by dropping number of customers acquired by 20% and half as many people behaving like the top 10%. 



For both cases, we want to answer how much can we lend upfront to receive the full 1.2× repayment by each month. So, for every month alculate cumulative cohort revenue through that month, then take 50% as the revenue available for repayment, then divide by 1.2 to calculate the maximum upfront loan supported.

I’ll calculate the loan ceiling for each month from cumulative cohort revenue. For the worse case, I’ll model 20% fewer customers overall, with the top-spender share falling from 10% to 5%. The remaining 95% will follow the observed behaviour of the other customers.

![Maximum upfront loan supported by repayment month](../assets/diagrams/cdnow_cohort_loan_capacity.png)

For each repayment deadline:

**Maximum upfront loan = cumulative cohort revenue × 50% ÷ 1.2**

The normal case replays the historical cohort exactly. For the worse case, I interpreted your assumptions as **20% fewer customers overall**, with **5% behaving like historical top spenders and 95% like the remaining customers**, preserving each group’s observed spending and timing.

| Repayment by end of month | Normal loan ($000) | Worse-case loan ($000) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 124.6 | 91.8 |
| 2 | 282.8 | 204.0 |
| 3 | 446.6 | 316.9 |
| 4 | 506.1 | 351.0 |
| 5 | 551.1 | 376.2 |
| 6 | 596.2 | 401.4 |
| 7 | 647.1 | 429.0 |
| 8 | 683.9 | 449.2 |
| 9 | 718.1 | 467.8 |
| 10 | 755.5 | 488.4 |
| 11 | 803.6 | 514.1 |
| 12 | 843.4 | 536.3 |
| 13 | 875.4 | 553.5 |
| 14 | 907.5 | 570.7 |
| 15 | 952.9 | 595.5 |
| 16 | 980.5 | 610.6 |
| 17 | 1,010.1 | 626.6 |
| 18 | **1,041.8** | **643.9** |

Month 1 is the start of the acquisition quarter, equivalent to January 1997 in the replay. Initial and repeat revenue both count toward repayment.

These are scenario-supported ceilings, assuming the full revenue share is paid by each month-end. The data does not establish how much marketing capital would produce either customer outcome.

[Download monthly calculations, including cumulative revenue and repayment available](../assets/diagrams/cdnow_cohort_loan_capacity.csv)

problem with this is that there is no CAC, ops cost, etc so its a little hard to really make any decisions here. Can you make an educated guess for a typical CAC in 1997 then output the minimum loan needed for the initial acquisition of all 23570 customers as well as the minimum number of months to get the full repayment for both base and worse case as previously mentioned.

I’ll look for historical acquisition-cost evidence, choose a working CAC assumption, and calculate the upfront acquisition loan and repayment month under both scenarios. I’ll keep acquisition cost separate from operating costs, which the transaction data doesn’t cover.

The historical evidence I found estimates CDNOW’s CAC at $30–$55 during 1998–2000, but doesn’t establish its actual 1997 CAC. I’ll use $40 per customer as a working assumption and show how the result changes at other CAC levels.

I’ll hold the loan fixed in the worse case: the same marketing budget produces 20% fewer customers and the weaker spending mix.

I’d use **$40 CAC per customer as a working assumption**, in nominal dollars. Published estimates place CDNOW’s CAC at **$30–$55 during 1998–2000**; $40 is a reasonable nearby-period proxy, **not a verified 1997 figure**. [Source: *Managing Customers as Investments*, pp. 59–60](https://ptgmedia.pearsoncmg.com/images/9780132161619/samplepages/0132161613.pdf).

Assuming the loan funds all acquisition spending upfront:

**Acquisition loan = 23,570 × $40 = $942,800**  
**Full repayment required = $942,800 × 1.2 = $1,131,360**

| Metric | Base case | Worse case |
|---|---:|---:|
| Upfront loan | $942,800 | $942,800 |
| Customers acquired | 23,570 | 18,856 |
| Effective CAC | $40 | $50 |
| First month reaching full 1.2× repayment | **Month 15** | **Not reached within 18 months** |
| Repayment available through month 18, before applying cap | $1,250,158 | $772,638 |

The worse case keeps the **same marketing budget**, but acquires 20% fewer customers and has a 5% top-spender mix, as previously modelled. It remains **$358,722 short** of full repayment at month 18. We cannot identify its eventual repayment month without forecasting beyond the available data.

The conclusion is sensitive to CAC:

| Assumed CAC | Acquisition loan | Base repayment month | Worse repayment month |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $25 — optimistic sensitivity | $589,250 | 6 | 15 |
| $30 | $707,100 | 9 | Not within 18 |
| **$40 — working assumption** | **$942,800** | **15** | **Not within 18** |
| $55 | $1,296,350 | Not within 18 | Not within 18 |

Months are counted from the start of the acquisition quarter. This is an **acquisition-only funding requirement**: inventory, fulfilment, operating costs and liquidity reserves would require additional funding. The calculations also assume CDNOW can remit the full 50% revenue share while meeting those costs.

Note that I am aware that we do not know of any other operating costs and what not, but we want to simplify the problem first with whatever information we do have.

Launch 2 subagents with 1 wanting to invest and the other not wanting to invest. Do not give the subagents any context apart from the raw data and the investment terms. Let them discuss and exchange messages up to 20 times before coming to their own conclusions.

Given those conclusions, use it to fact check and argue against my own thought process which is as follows:

Since the data available is only for 1 cohort, then the entire invest or not question boils down to if cdnow is able to replicate their campaign to get the same revenue targets.

This boils down to the quality of their customers attained which we can conclude the following:

1. repeat customers form a majority in revenue share, but there is a declining trend given that 14.9% of customers repurchase on month 1 but only 6.3% do the same on month 17.
2. among the repeat customers, there are the top 10% who account for 50.9% of revenue.

Assuming we do want to invest, we do want to project base and worse case scenarios to calculate how long it would take to get our full repayment. Base case is the exact same and the worse case is a 20% drop in customers with only a 5% top spender mix. Since CAC was not known, a web search found cdnow's CAC is at $30–$55 during 1998–2000. With a range of CAC, we now a range of minimum loan needed to acquire the same number of customers with hopefully the same behaviour.

Since we are investing in the future, I will take the $55 CAC mark as the working assumption in which case we have already projected that within the 18 months worth of data we have, we won't be able to get back the full repayment. Therefore, I will recommend not investing until we get data that tracks customer behaviour over a longer period and also change the investment terms to not restrict within a cohort since the 10% top spender accounting for 50.9% of revenue could be compounded across various cohorts and may make the investment more worth it.

I’ll launch two agents with opposing starting positions, giving them only the raw-data location and investment terms. They’ll exchange up to 20 messages total and reach separate conclusions. I’ll then use their findings to challenge your reasoning within the simplified model.

Two fact-check corrections already stand out: repeat purchases generated 69.0% of this cohort’s observed revenue, while the 50.9% figure belongs to the top 10% of all customers, ranked by total spending. Also, an 18-month observation window is not a contractual repayment deadline. The agents are still debating what those limits imply for the investment decision.

**Your recommendation to defer is defensible, but the strongest argument is the mismatch between acquisition funding and repayment capacity—not concentration by itself.** I’ll stay within the simplified revenue model.

The two agents received only the raw data and investment terms, with opposing starting positions. They exchanged **8 substantive messages** and independently concluded:

- **Investment advocate:** smaller advances could repay quickly under historical behaviour, so the structure can work. But the data doesn’t establish that those advances could finance a comparable future cohort.
- **Investment skeptic:** defer commitment until the loan amount and achievable acquisition outcome are supported. Declining purchasing activity makes reliance on later revenue less secure.

Neither agent received your thesis, our forecasts, or the researched CAC figures.

**1. Replicating the campaign is only part of the investment question.**

Even perfectly replicated customer behaviour may be insufficient if acquiring those customers requires too much capital. Under these terms:

**Every $1 lent requires $2.40 of cohort revenue to achieve full repayment.**

The central question is therefore: **how much cohort revenue does each acquisition dollar produce, and how quickly?**

The agents’ strongest counterargument to rejecting the investment outright was loan size: the historical revenue supports full repayment of approximately **$446,586 by month 3**, but only **$1,041,798 by month 18**. That demonstrates repayment capacity at smaller advances; it doesn’t demonstrate that smaller advances could acquire all 23,570 customers.

**2. Your behavioural conclusions need two corrections.**

Repeat purchases contributed **69.0% of this cohort’s observed revenue**. Monthly purchasing activity generally declined, from **14.9% in month 1 to 6.3% in month 15**, when all customers remain observable. Month 17 also shows 6.3%, but includes January entrants only.

The **50.9% figure belongs to the top-spending 10% of all customers**, including their initial and repeat purchases. It is not the top 10% among repeat customers. Moreover, these customers were identified retrospectively; we haven’t shown how to identify or acquire similar customers beforehand.

**3. Using $55 CAC supports deferral—but doesn’t prove ultimate non-repayment.**

The published $30–$55 range concerns **1998–2000**, so $55 is a chosen stress assumption for this exercise, rather than an established future CAC or upper bound. [Source: *Managing Customers as Investments*, pp. 59–60](https://ptgmedia.pearsoncmg.com/images/9780132161619/samplepages/0132161613.pdf).

At $55 CAC:

| Metric | Base case | Worse case |
|---|---:|---:|
| Fixed upfront loan | $1,296,350 | $1,296,350 |
| Required 1.2× repayment | $1,555,620 | $1,555,620 |
| Repayment available through month 18 | $1,250,158 | $772,638 |
| Shortfall against full repayment | **$305,462** | **$782,982** |

The worse case holds funding fixed while acquiring 20% fewer customers and reducing the top-spender mix to 5%.

However, **18 months is our data boundary, not a contractual deadline**. We can conclude that neither scenario demonstrates full repayment within 18 months. We cannot conclude that either will never repay. Longer tracking would help estimate the remaining revenue and repayment duration; additional independent cohorts would help assess repeatability.

**4. Pooling cohorts could improve protection, but concentration does not compound returns.**

If ten equally funded cohorts repeat the same economics, revenue and capital requirements both increase tenfold. The repayment ratio remains unchanged.

Pooling could help diversify uneven outcomes or let stronger cohorts cover weaker ones. That benefit depends on how differently cohorts perform and which revenues secure which loans. **The existence of top spenders alone does not establish that benefit.**

A stronger version of your recommendation would be:

> At an assumed $55 CAC, the required $1.296 million loan does not achieve full 1.2× repayment within the observed 18 months under either scenario. I would defer commitment until we have evidence on achievable acquisition cost, performance across additional cohorts, and the revenue tail needed to estimate repayment duration. I would evaluate pooled repayment rights as potential additional protection, rather than assume pooling improves the underlying economics.
